summary: Defines an algorithm that finds, in an email message, the identity of the party that appears to have most directly caused the message to be delivered. This identity is the Purported Responsible Address. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: It is a rule for looking at an email's headers and deciding which address most likely was the one that actually sent it.

subtitle: An algorithm for finding who appears to have sent an email by examining its headers

tldr.problem: When an email is forwarded or relayed through multiple systems, figuring out who actually submitted it requires examining message headers, but those headers can be complex and may not exist or may be malformed.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a precise algorithm that looks at specific header fields in a specific order: Resent-Sender or Resent-From first (for forwarded messages), then Sender, then From, returning the first valid email address found.
tldr.outcome: Systems like SMTP servers and spam filters have a consistent way to determine the Purported Responsible Address (PRA), enabling them to validate the sender's authorization independently of protocol-level data.

facts.label: Returns
facts.value: First valid single mailbox or error

today: RFC 4407 is Historic. It was published alongside RFC 4405 and RFC 4406 as part of an experimental approach to email sender authentication. The IESG noted that while these documents are useful for understanding different approaches, there was no technical consensus, and these mechanisms did not become mainstream. Other technologies like SPF and DKIM eventually became more widely deployed for sender verification.

sections.title: Why We Need This Algorithm
sections.content:
Most emails travel directly from sender to recipient, but many messages are resent by forwarding agents, mailing list servers, or other intermediaries. These intermediaries add Resent-* headers to track the forwarding. Some messages may also have a Sender header distinct from the From header—for example, when a news website forwards an article on behalf of a reader.

The Purported Responsible Address (PRA) is the identity that appears, from the headers, to have most directly caused the message to be delivered. This is useful for validation, but only if all systems determine the PRA the same way. This document defines a precise algorithm for that determination.
sections.eli5: When an email is forwarded, it gets new headers. This rule says which header to look at first to figure out who really sent it.

sections.title: The PRA Extraction Algorithm
sections.content:
The algorithm works in six steps. Step 1: look for the first non-empty Resent-Sender header. If found and not preceded by Resent-From with Received headers in between, return it. Step 2: if Resent-Sender is not found or failed the conditions, look for Resent-From and return it. Step 3: if no Resent headers, look for all Sender headers. If exactly one exists, continue to Step 5. If more than one, go to Step 6. Step 4: if no Sender header, look at all From headers. If exactly one exists, continue to Step 5. Otherwise go to Step 6. Step 5: check if the selected header is malformed (multiple mailboxes, no domain, etc.). If valid, return it. If malformed, go to Step 6. Step 6: the message is ill-formed and no PRA can be determined.

A header field is considered empty only if it contains nothing but whitespace. The algorithm correctly handles Resent blocks as defined by RFC 2822, and provides guidance for systems that need to accept non-standard messages.
sections.eli5: First check for a Resent-Sender, then Resent-From, then Sender, then From. Return the first one that exists and looks valid. If none work, the headers are too broken to tell.

sections.title: Security and Trustworthiness
sections.content:
The PRA is extracted from headers that have historically not been verified. Anyone using the PRA for security or authenticity purposes MUST be aware that the headers might be fraudulent, malicious, malformed, or incorrect. Headers can be faked, so the PRA is not proof of identity—it is only "purported" to be the responsible address.

If the PRA is used as part of an authentication mechanism, the email SHOULD NOT be displayed with an indication of authenticity (positive or negative) without also displaying the PRA header field itself. This ensures the user can see the basis for any authentication decision.
sections.eli5: Headers can be faked, so the PRA is just a claim about who sent it, not proof. The system must double-check it somehow, and the user should see which header was used.

sections.title: Example Scenarios
sections.content:
For a direct email from Alice to Bob with only a From header, the algorithm returns the From address. For an email from Alice forwarded by a mailing list, if Resent-From is present, that address is the PRA (the mailing list). For an email with multiple Sender headers (malformed), or multiple From headers (not single sender), the algorithm returns no PRA.

If Alice's email is forwarded, modified, and forwarded again, each forwarding agent adds its own Resent-From, and the algorithm returns the most recent one. This correctly identifies who most recently introduced the message into the mail system.
sections.eli5: A regular email returns its From address. A forwarded email returns the forwarder's address. Multiple confusing headers or missing headers mean the system cannot tell.
